name: Iris Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Iris Tanaka, 43, and I operate a shuttle car underground at a large mine. I check the brakes, take ore from the cutting area to the conveyor, and listen hard for the spotter on the radio. I'm still a junior driver; a tight turn can take me two goes when an experienced hand does it in one. My partner drives a town bus, our two children are in school, and we pay a mortgage; we have about three months of expenses saved, but I don't like dipping into it. I like the crew looking out for one another and dislike being hurried through a blind corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small software changes should be checked by the workers who use the roads and radios. I would keep a human spotter near the conveyor entrance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own shift probably survives this mild AI picture. I still worry about a bus timetable cut reducing my partner's hours before we need the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking shuttle-car brakes at the start of every shift and record faults in the log. I'd attend the union safety meeting next month to raise the blind corner by the conveyor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI part leaves me mostly steady, but our household has two wages that can change. Three months of savings is comfort until you start spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why raise that corner now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A truck came out of it too fast last week, and my spotter had to wave me back. I want the union to ask for a marked waiting point before someone is hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have never used an AI tool. I would rather ask the spotter or the maintenance crew when a warning light comes on.

say: I'd say **small software changes** should be checked by the workers who use the roads and radios.
I would keep a **human spotter** near the conveyor entrance.
think: My own shift probably survives this **mild AI** picture.
I still worry about a **bus timetable cut** reducing my partner's hours before we need the savings.
do: Keep checking **shuttle-car brakes** at the start of every shift and record faults in the log.
Attend the **union safety meeting** next month to raise the blind corner by the conveyor.
feel: **Uneasy** about household hours and road safety, though her shift seems secure.
S0.quote: Three months of savings is comfort until you start spending it.
fieldNote: She regards **mild AI** as secondary to mine safety and her partner's possible bus hours.
Her union request concerns a **specific blind corner**, not a general claim that technology is unsafe.

steps.text: Keep checking shuttle-car brakes and logging faults each shift
Attend the union safety meeting about the conveyor blind corner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our union representative to demand a safety review before software changes dispatch instructions. The drivers should be able to stop a run when a route looks wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning staff may be cut first, but a leaner crew could push more trips onto junior drivers. My partner's bus wage and our savings would help for a while, not indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring my shift log to the next union meeting and ask for a vote on dispatch safeguards. I'd keep working the shuttle route while checking the weekly roster for fewer paid trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cross when efficiency means a driver gets less time to check a brake. I also feel nervous, because the new dispatch system may arrive whether the crew agrees or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the dispatch change acceptable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Give drivers a way to report a blocked route and keep a named person who can override a bad instruction. I need to see the system work in our tunnels before I trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine makes it part of the job, I would learn the buttons from another driver. I would not call that an exciting new career; I want a safe route and a paid shift.

The drivers should be able to **stop a run** when a route looks wrong.
think: Planning staff may be cut first, but a leaner crew could push **more trips** onto junior drivers.
My partner's bus wage and our **savings** would help for a while, not indefinitely.
do: Bring my **shift log** to the next union meeting and ask for a vote on dispatch safeguards.
Keep working the **shuttle route** while checking the weekly roster for fewer paid trips.
feel: **Anxious** about thinner crews and faster trips, with a union channel for response.
S1.quote: I want a safe route and a paid shift.
fieldNote: She connects **thinking-task automation** to dispatch cuts and greater pressure on physical drivers.
She will learn required controls once proven by **another driver**, while resisting claims that this secures her future.

steps.text: Bring the shift log to a union vote on dispatch safeguards
Keep driving and check the weekly roster for paid trips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI in 2028 may empty the dispatch room before robots can drive underground. Our union must get robot dates and terms in writing before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45, I would still owe the mortgage when thinking AI arrives. Robots around 2031 could take my car shift, and three months of savings would run out quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union representative to seek a written agreement on paid redeployment before robot trials. I'd keep my paid shuttle shifts during 2029 and look at posted mine vacancies each Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened, and I am not ready to pretend a computer course fixes it. The sight of an empty shuttle seat would mean somebody's rent or mortgage stopped being paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which vacancy might you take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would consider a posted stores job if it paid close to my current wage, but I know I lack the stock records experience. I would apply only after asking the stores lead what training is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your partner's income cover the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bus wage could buy us a little time, but not carry the mortgage and both children for long. I would ask about public wage support if the mine actually cut my shifts.

say: I'd say **AGI in 2028** may empty the dispatch room before robots can drive underground.
Our union must get **robot dates and terms** in writing before 2031.
think: At **45**, I would still owe the mortgage when thinking AI arrives.
Robots around **2031** could take my car shift, and three months of savings would run out quickly.
do: Ask the **union representative** to seek a written agreement on paid redeployment before robot trials.
Keep my **paid shuttle shifts** during 2029 and look at posted mine vacancies each Friday.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely robot threat to her wage within three years.
S2.quote: The sight of an empty shuttle seat would mean somebody's rent or mortgage stopped being paid.
fieldNote: She sees the **2028 dispatch shock** and later direct robot threat as different events.
Her first response is **collective bargaining** for paid redeployment, while a stores application requires a real vacancy and training.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate paid redeployment before robot trials
Keep paid shuttle shifts through the first year after 2028
Apply for a stores vacancy if pay and training are adequate
Ask about public wage support if mine shifts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years gives the union time to bargain for training with wages attached. I would want human safety checks kept while robots are tested underground around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 in 2031, and the children would be older but still depend on us. A funded transfer could work; an unpaid course could eat our savings before any robot arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union for paid training terms in its next mine agreement. I'd apply for a mine safety assistant opening if it includes supervised instruction and similar pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could stand a longer countdown if I knew the bargaining had a real result. I would still wake up wondering whether the mine has room for all the drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a safety assistant role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the blind corners from driving them, but I don't know the inspection rules yet. I would need a supervisor to teach me before I signed a safety report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in the year after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue my shuttle shifts while they still need a driver and check the job board with the union representative. My children would be teenagers then, so I would not count on school costs disappearing.

say: I'd tell the crew **five years** gives the union time to bargain for training with wages attached.
I would want **human safety checks** kept while robots are tested underground around 2034.
think: I would be **48 in 2031**, and the children would be older but still depend on us.
A funded transfer could work; an **unpaid course** could eat our savings before any robot arrives.
do: Ask the union for **paid training terms** in its next mine agreement.
Apply for a **mine safety assistant** opening if it includes supervised instruction and similar pay.
feel: **Anxious** about limited transfer places despite a longer bargaining window.
S3.quote: I would not count on school costs disappearing.
fieldNote: She uses the five years for **union bargaining** and a conditional safety-job application.
She distinguishes her **local route knowledge** from formal inspection skill and expects teenage children to cost money.

steps.text: Ask the union to bargain for paid training in the next mine agreement
Apply for safety assistant work if pay and supervision are adequate
Continue paid shuttle shifts during the first year after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years of notice is enough to make employers fund a proper transition. I would press for public support for mine towns when robot cars spread around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, I would not be ready to stop earning. Our children may be grown by 2039, but the mortgage and our own food bill will remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stand for a union training committee place at the next election if a seat opens. I'd put a fixed monthly amount into our reserve while both mine and bus hours hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The decade helps, yet I do not want ten years of meetings that end in a printed promise. I would feel better with training places and income protection written into an agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine offered paid instruction for underground equipment inspection, I would enrol even though I dislike new systems. I would need a worker beside me at first, not a screen that says I am certified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask of public leaders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask them to fund temporary wages and local training if the mine removes many jobs at once. A mine town cannot replace hundreds of pay packets with a leaflet.

say: I'd say **ten years of notice** is enough to make employers fund a proper transition.
I would press for **public support** for mine towns when robot cars spread around 2039.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I would not be ready to stop earning.
Our children may be grown by **2039**, but the mortgage and our own food bill will remain.
do: Stand for a **union training committee** place at the next election if a seat opens.
Put a **fixed monthly amount** into our reserve while both mine and bus hours hold.
feel: **Uneasy** about prolonged uncertainty, with time for bargaining and a reserve.
S4.quote: A mine town cannot replace hundreds of pay packets with a leaflet.
fieldNote: Her decade plan combines **union office**, conditional paid inspection training, and a household reserve.
She expects the **robot date** to affect the whole town and asks for temporary wages tied to local training.

steps.text: Stand for a union training committee seat if one opens
Save a fixed monthly amount while both household rosters hold
Enrol in paid inspection instruction if the mine offers it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the robots could reach my shuttle car around 2031 before we bargain a decent landing. A written agreement on paid redeployment and public wage support if jobs are cut would help. I would also want proper supervised training, not a certificate sent by email.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the first training place. Junior drivers like me might be last on the list unless the union makes the selection rules fair.

headlineQuote: Junior drivers like me might be last on the list unless the union makes the selection rules fair.
portrait: Iris is a **43-year-old junior** underground shuttle-car driver who relies on spotters and careful brake checks.
Her partner drives a bus; **three months of savings**, two school-age children, and a mortgage give some room but no lasting shield.
She avoids **AI tools** and wants workers to test dispatch changes and retain authority to stop unsafe runs.
She pursues **union bargaining** for paid redeployment and supervised training before robot cars threaten her shift.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time for a fair agreement before robots threaten her shuttle-car wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid redeployment**, supervised training, and public wage support after actual cuts would give her household time.
